readings.title: The old cinema opens its doors again
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A town bought an empty cinema with plans for a public arts space. Residents remembered films there, but the building also had serious access problems. The central difficulty was nostalgia hiding practical building limits. Early meetings praised the painted ceiling while saying little about narrow entrances, heating costs or the needs of wheelchair users. The organizers knew that a tidy plan in an office might not match what happened in an ordinary week.

The group first tried guided visits with different residents. Architects walked through the building with former staff, younger visitors and people who used mobility aids, noting barriers and valued details. They therefore listened to people who used the place at different times, including those who seldom attended formal meetings.

The trial showed the side entrance was easier to adapt. It was less impressive than the front doors, yet offered a practical way to reach the main hall without steps. In response, the group adopted a phased repair preserving key features. The council planned an accessible entrance first and delayed decorative work until essential safety and heating questions were settled. The notes did not remove every disagreement, but they made the reasons for the next decision easier to explain.

The broader lesson was clear: a historic place must serve present users. People could cherish memories of the cinema while asking whether a renovated building would welcome the whole community. Keeping a record of small changes also helped the team distinguish a temporary setback from a lasting problem. For the people involved in the old cinema opens its doors again, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: Voices from a fishing harbour
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A museum invited former harbour workers to describe changes in local fishing. Their stories added details absent from official shipping records. The central difficulty was different memories of the same busy season. Two contributors remembered opposite reasons for a long delay, and the museum did not want to present either account as certain. A first impression was not enough to tell the whole story, because different people approached the service in different ways.

The group first tried recorded interviews alongside written sources. Staff dated each recollection, checked surviving notices and invited speakers to review how their words would be used. The team compared comments with direct observations rather than assuming that the loudest opinion represented everyone.

The trial showed personal accounts supplied unique working details. The records listed boat movements, but only interviews described how families prepared food and waited for news. In response, the group adopted labels explaining what each source can show. The display kept the conflicting memories and showed visitors the difference between a personal view and an official document. Some suggestions were inexpensive, while others would have required a change to staffing or equipment.

The broader lesson was clear: historical evidence gains strength through comparison. The museum treated disagreement as a reason to ask better questions rather than a reason to discard the speakers. The final proposal remained open to revision when new information became available. For the people involved in voices from a fishing harbour, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: A warehouse becomes a study centre
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A brick warehouse near the station had stood empty for years. A college proposed using it for adult study and community meetings. The central difficulty was a large floor plan with poor quiet spaces. The open interior looked flexible, but echoes made conversation difficult and evening learners needed places to concentrate. Several participants valued the original aim even though they questioned the first method chosen to reach it.

The group first tried temporary rooms made with movable screens. Before permanent work, staff held sample classes and meetings in several layouts and asked users about sound and comfort. Short conversations after the activity revealed details that a written form had failed to capture.

The trial showed small groups needed stronger sound separation. A layout suitable for public talks did not work for language classes, where learners had to hear one another clearly. In response, the group adopted a mix of quiet rooms and an open hall. The final design preserved the visible brick structure while adding enclosed teaching spaces and simple signs to guide visitors. The people responsible made their limits clear and invited others to describe any unintended effects.

The broader lesson was clear: adaptive reuse depends on activities as well as architecture. Keeping an old building useful required attention to the ordinary sounds and movements of its new occupants. This approach gave the group a practical basis for its next round of work. For the people involved in a warehouse becomes a study centre, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: Who can use a local archive?
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A town archive held photographs and plans of familiar streets. Researchers used it regularly, but residents rarely visited. The central difficulty was unclear rules for first-time archive visitors. The website listed opening hours but did not explain how to request a photograph or whether an appointment was required. The project began on a small scale so that its organizers could learn before making a permanent commitment.

The group first tried short observation sessions with new users. Staff invited residents to find one family photograph and noted the questions they asked at the counter and online. They noted both benefits and costs, including the time that volunteers or staff needed to give.

The trial showed a simple request guide removed uncertainty. Most visitors could manage the search once they saw an example of a request and knew how long retrieval might take. In response, the group adopted step-by-step guidance and monthly open hours. The archive added a short illustrated guide and offered a regular session for people who wanted help exploring its collection. The public summary described what had changed and what questions had not yet been answered.

The broader lesson was clear: public collections need understandable entry points. Preserving records mattered, but helping people discover and request them made the archive more useful to its community. Readers could therefore judge the decision by its evidence rather than by a promise of perfect results. For the people involved in who can use a local archive?, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
People often support the restoration of an old building because it carries memories of earlier generations. Yet a building that is beautiful in photographs may be difficult to use today. A town considered turning its former cinema into a public arts space. Visits with residents showed that the front entrance had steps and the large hall was costly to heat. The side entrance offered a better route for people using wheelchairs. Planners therefore decided to improve access and safety before beginning decorative work. They kept features that gave the cinema its character, while making room for new activities. Respect for history does not require ignoring the needs of present users.
translation.explanation: 注意because原因、while并列对比及does not require结构。
translation.referenceAnswer: 人们常支持修复旧建筑，因为它承载着前几代人的记忆。然而，在照片中美丽的建筑如今可能并不好用。一个城镇考虑把旧电影院改造成公共艺术空间。与居民共同参观后，规划者发现正门有台阶，大厅取暖成本也很高。侧门为使用轮椅的人提供了更好的通道。因此，规划者决定先改善出入便利和安全，再开展装饰工程。他们保留了赋予电影院特色的部分，同时为新活动留出空间。尊重历史并不意味着忽略当下使用者的需求。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to a council proposing how an old cinema could become a useful arts centre while keeping its historic character. Mention access, safety, and one feature worth preserving.
writing.explanation: 范文兼顾无障碍、安全与历史特色。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Council Members,
The old cinema could become a lively arts centre if the project begins with the needs of future visitors. I suggest inviting residents, performers and people who use mobility aids to walk through the building with architects. Their comments would help identify the safest route to the main hall and the spaces that are difficult to reach. Heating and fire safety should be addressed before decorative work begins.
At the same time, the painted ceiling is a feature many residents remember. It could be carefully restored and included in short information displays about the building. A phased plan would make costs easier to explain: first improve access and safety, then prepare rooms for performances and classes. The council should publish the stages and invite comments after each one.
Yours sincerely,
A local resident
